stances.claim: Cumulative jurisprudence across 2003, 2012, and 2017 SC/SBN decisions has systematically established the legal basis for forfeiting Marcos ill-gotten wealth: the $304,372.43 lawful income threshold, $658+ million in bank deposits, Arelma S.A. assets, and now the Malacañang Collection jewelry.

The 14-category $5-billion wealth listing from the 1991 PCGG petition -- now incorporated into the 2017 SC decision footnotes -- remains the most comprehensive inventory of alleged Marcos ill-gotten wealth.
stances.rhetorical_move: comprehensive-inventory framing showing the scale of alleged wealth

notable_anecdotes: The Marcoses arriving in Honolulu with P27,744,535 in Philippine peso bills, $4M in foreign currencies and jewelry, and P46.4M in Certificates of Time Deposits seized by US customs -- physicalizing the wealth through a border-crossing moment.

The gap between Marcos's officially recognized lawful income of $304,372.43 over 21 years and the $658+ million in bank deposits plus the $5B total estimate -- making the magnitude of alleged ill-gotten wealth viscerally clear.
The $17M in paintings and silverware sold at US auction plus $23.9M in Malacañang jewelry and decorative arts -- cultural assets as corruption evidence.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reviews the most recent jurisprudence on Marcos ill-gotten wealth -- Estate of Marcos v. Republic (January 18, 2017, CJ Sereno) -- in the context of Edsa@31. The decision affirmed a 2014 Sandiganbayan ruling (J. De la Cruz) that the Malacañang Collection jewelry was ill-gotten and forfeited in favor of the Republic. It recalled that Republic v. Sandiganbayan (July 15, 2003) unanimously fixed the Marcoses' known lawful income from 1965 to 1986 at only $304,372.43, with all assets above that threshold deemed ill-gotten -- including $658,175,373.60 in bank deposits forfeited in the same 2003 case. The 2012 Marcos Jr. v. Republic decision had separately forfeited Arelma S.A. assets of $3,369,975 (as of 1983) plus interest. The 2017 decision incorporated in its footnotes the 1991 PCGG petition (civil case 0141) listing 14 categories of alleged ill-gotten wealth 'approximated at US$5B,' spanning holding companies, agro-industrial ventures, land, buildings, condominiums, cash, paintings and silverware sold at US auction ($17M) and found in Malacañang ($23.9M), Philippine peso bills and foreign currency seized by US customs in Honolulu ($4M and P46.4M in time deposits), SBTC deposits (over P974M and $6.5M), Traders Royal Bank deposits (over P1B), and secret Swiss bank accounts as the 'primary and principal object of this petition.'
